name: Losar in Kalimpong
summary: Tibetan New Year in a town that has sheltered Tibetan traders and refugees for over a century. Monasteries on Durpin, Tirpai and in the bazaar fill with butter lamps, prayer flags go up across the ridges, and families visit with khapse biscuits and chhang.
body: Kalimpong's Tibetan story is older than 1959. For decades before the 1962 war closed Jelep La, Tibetan wool traders and their mule drivers wintered in the town, and some families stayed. After 1959 many more came as refugees, and monks rebuilt their institutions here, from Zang Dhok Palri on Durpin hill, consecrated by the 14th Dalai Lama in 1976, to the smaller gompas of Tirpai and the bazaar.

Losar falls on the first day of the first Tibetan lunar month, usually in February and sometimes in early March. The days before are for cleaning houses and making khapse, fried pastry twists. On the day itself families visit the monastery early, then each other. New prayer flags are hung on the ridges above town, and you will see them flapping on Durpin and Deolo for weeks after.

For visitors it is a quiet, family festival rather than a show. You will see the most at the monasteries in the morning: prayers, butter lamps and long queues of people in their best chuba. Some monasteries hold masked cham dances in the days around the new year, but dates and rituals differ between them, so ask at the monastery office a few days ahead.
tips: Visit Zang Dhok Palri on Durpin early on Losar morning, when families come to pray, and walk around the building clockwise.
Shops and Tibetan restaurants may close for two or three days, so keep some snacks and check opening times in advance.
Losar dates follow the Tibetan lunar calendar and move each year: check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: When is Losar celebrated in Kalimpong?
faqs.a: Losar falls on the first day of the Tibetan lunar year, usually in February, occasionally early March. The exact date changes every year and can differ by a day between Tibetan and Sherpa or Bhutanese calendars. Check a Tibetan calendar or ask your hotel before booking, and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can tourists visit monasteries during Losar?
faqs.a: Yes, visitors are generally welcome at Kalimpong's monasteries during Losar, as long as you are respectful. Dress modestly, walk clockwise, keep your voice low in the prayer hall and ask before photographing monks or rituals. Some inner rooms may be closed. A small donation or a white khata scarf is appreciated but not expected.

faqs.q: Are there mask dances at Losar in Kalimpong?
faqs.a: Some monasteries hold cham mask dances around the new year, but it differs between monasteries and years, and many of the larger cham festivals in the region happen at other times of the Tibetan calendar. Ask at the monastery office a few days ahead for the year's programme and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is February a good time to visit Kalimpong?
faqs.a: Yes. February is dry and cold, about 6–15 °C in town, and mornings are often clear for Kanchenjunga from Deolo and Durpin. Lava and Rishyap can see frost or the odd snowfall. Hotel prices are lower than in October and May, and Losar gives you a festival week if the dates line up.

name: Dashain and Tihar in Kalimpong
when: Oct–Nov, Dashain then Tihar (Hindu lunar calendar)
summary: The biggest festival season of the Nepali-speaking hills. Dashain brings red tika, jamara barley shoots and family visits; Tihar, two to three weeks later, brings oil lamps, marigold garlands, garlands for dogs and the deusi-bhailo songs that groups sing from house to house.
body: For most families in Kalimpong, Dashain is the year's main holiday. It runs alongside Durga Puja in the plains, and on Tika day, the tenth day, elders put a mix of rice, curd and red colour on the foreheads of younger relatives, along with the pale yellow jamara shoots grown from barley seed over the previous nine days. Families travel long distances to receive tika from their grandparents, and shops close.

Tihar follows two to three weeks later, around Diwali. Over five days the hills honour crows, dogs, cows and oxen in turn, and on Bhai Tika sisters bless their brothers. Houses are lit with oil lamps and strings of lights. In the evenings, groups of young people go from house to house singing deusi and bhailo songs and collecting small gifts, often for a club or a cause.

For visitors, this is also the busiest season of the year. Families from Kolkata and the rest of Bengal come up for the Puja holidays, rooms fill and taxi fares rise. If you want to see the festivals, book early and travel on the less busy days in between.
tips: Book rooms and NJP trains six to eight weeks ahead for the Puja and Diwali weeks, and expect higher taxi fares.
On Tika day many shops and jeep stands are quiet; plan a rest day instead of a long transfer.
Dates follow the Hindu lunar calendar and move each year: check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: When are Dashain and Tihar in 2026?
faqs.a: Dashain usually falls in late September or October, with Tika day matching Bijaya Dashami, the end of Durga Puja. Tihar follows two to three weeks later and matches Diwali in October or November. Exact dates change each year, so look up the Nepali calendar for the year you travel and check current status before you travel.

Dashain is mainly a family festival, so there is no big public event to attend. Homestay families often invite guests to watch tika being given, and some will offer you tika too. Accept with both hands, and it is polite to bring a small gift of sweets or fruit. In town you will see swings, kite flying and markets full of new clothes.

Deusi and bhailo are call-and-response songs sung during Tihar. Groups of girls (bhailo) and boys or mixed groups (deusi) visit houses and shops in the evening, sing, dance and bless the household, which gives them money, rice or sweets. In Kalimpong the groups often collect for clubs or charities. Listen from your homestay doorway; hosts usually welcome it.

faqs.q: Is October too crowded to visit Kalimpong?
faqs.a: The Durga Puja and Diwali weeks are crowded and pricier, but the rest of October and November are among the best weeks of the year, with clear skies and dry roads. Stay in a village such as Sillery Gaon or Icchey Gaon to avoid town traffic, book early, and check current status before you travel.

name: Namsoong, the Lepcha New Year
summary: The Lepcha New Year, celebrated in Kalimpong and the Lepcha villages around it in December or January. Prayers led by Lepcha priests, traditional dress, food and dances mark the turn of the year for the people who were in these hills first.
body: The Lepcha, who call themselves Rong, are the oldest people of the Kalimpong and Sikkim hills, and their villages, from Lolegaon to Charkhole, still dot the Kalimpong ridges. Namsoong is their New Year, timed by the Lepcha lunar calendar to fall in December or January.

In Kalimpong the celebration is organised by Lepcha community bodies over several days, with rituals led by Lepcha priests, cultural programmes, exhibitions of traditional dress, crafts and food, and songs and dances. The story most often told around Namsoong is a Lepcha legend of the victory of light over a demon of darkness; take it as the community's own story, told in its own way.

For travellers this is a chance to see Lepcha culture as a living thing rather than a museum piece: the striped handwoven dress, the cane hats, the food. Programmes are organised locally and the venue and dates are announced late, so ask your hotel or at the Lepcha Museum in town.
tips: Ask at your hotel or the Lepcha Museum in Kalimpong for the year's programme and venue.
Ask before photographing rituals and elders, and follow the organisers' lead on where to stand.
Dates follow the Lepcha lunar calendar and change each year: check current status before you travel.

faqs.a: Namsoong is the New Year festival of the Lepcha people, the oldest community of the Kalimpong and Sikkim hills. It is celebrated in December or January according to the Lepcha calendar, with rituals led by Lepcha priests, traditional dress, food, music and dance. In Kalimpong it is organised by community associations over several days.

faqs.q: Can tourists attend Namsoong in Kalimpong?
faqs.a: Public cultural programmes are usually open to all, and visitors are welcome if they are respectful. Rituals may be more private. Ask the organisers before photographing, dress modestly and follow where locals sit or stand. The programme and venue are announced locally each year, so check current status before you travel.

Namsoong falls in December or January, following the Lepcha lunar calendar, so the exact dates move each year. It often overlaps with the Christmas and New Year holiday period, when Kalimpong is cold, dry and clear. Ask locally or watch Lepcha community announcements, and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Where can I learn about Lepcha culture in Kalimpong?
faqs.a: Start at the Lepcha Museum on the edge of Kalimpong town, then visit a Lepcha village such as Lolegaon or Charkhole and stay in a homestay. If your dates allow, attend Namsoong in December or January, or the 20 December gathering at Damsang fort near Pedong for the Lepcha chief Gaeboo Achyok.

name: Gaeboo Achyok Day at Damsang fort
summary: Every 20 December, Lepchas from Kalimpong, Darjeeling and Sikkim gather at the ruins of Damsang fort near Pedong to mark the birth anniversary of Gaeboo Achyok, the 17th-century Lepcha chief who fought the Bhutanese for these hills.
body: Gaeboo Achyok is the most celebrated hero in Lepcha history. In the second half of the 17th century he led a Lepcha principality based at Damsang, above Pedong, and tried to hold the Kalimpong hills against the expanding kingdom of Bhutan, making an alliance with Tibet. The wars ended with his capture and execution, and Bhutan held Kalimpong until the Treaty of Sinchula in 1865.

His fort, Damsang Gadi, is now a ruin of stone walls on a forested ridge a few kilometres from Pedong. The date usually given for it is 1690, though historians disagree on the exact years of his rule. Lepcha lore says spirits carried the large, smooth round stones of its walls up from the Reshi river; that is a story, and a good one.

On 20 December each year, Lepcha families and community groups come to the fort for the anniversary of his birth, with rituals, speeches, songs and traditional dress. It is a community observance first, not a tourist event, but respectful visitors are generally welcome.
tips: Stay in Pedong or Sillery Gaon the night before, as the walk or drive up to Damsang starts early.
Wear good shoes: the last stretch to the ruins is a rough forest path.
Arrangements are made by community groups each year: check current status before you travel.

faqs.a: Gaeboo Achyok was a Lepcha chieftain who led a principality based at Damsang, near present-day Pedong, in the second half of the 17th century. He resisted Bhutanese expansion into the Kalimpong hills and allied with Tibet, but was eventually captured and executed. Lepchas honour him as their greatest hero and mark his birth anniversary on 20 December.

faqs.q: How do I reach Damsang fort from Pedong?
faqs.a: Damsang fort is a few kilometres above Pedong. Hire a local taxi from Pedong bazaar for about ₹600–1,000 return to the nearest road point, then walk the last stretch on a forest path, 15–30 minutes. You can also walk from Pedong, Sillery Gaon or Icchey Gaon with a local guide, which takes a half day.

faqs.q: Is anything left of Damsang fort?
faqs.a: Only ruins: low walls and scattered dressed stones on a forested hilltop, with views over the Pedong and Rhenock hills. It fell to ruin after the Anglo-Bhutan war of 1864. Go for the story and the setting, not for a standing castle, and do not climb on the walls.

faqs.q: Can tourists attend the 20 December gathering?
faqs.a: Yes, respectful visitors are generally welcome, but remember that it is a community commemoration. Dress warmly and modestly, ask before photographing rituals or elders, and stay out of the way of the organisers. Programme timings are set locally each year, so check current status before you travel.
